newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols rise, eyes on low-delta yen puts.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols rise, eyes on low-delta yen puts.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options edged higher in moderate U.S. trade, with a lot of interest in back-end low-delta yen puts after some mysterious large buying last week, dealers said.
Besides the back months, the short maturities were also firmer, resulting in a very flat volatility curve at the front end and very steep six month and out.
Traders said a general flattening and declining of the whole curve in the past few months now seemed to be halting.
"The tide is probably changing," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen stood at 6.8/6.9 percent, up from 6.5/6.8 late on Friday. Three and six-month volatilities stood at 7.05/7.15 and 7.95/8.05 percent respectively.
Traders said the rise in the front end was partly due to the dollar's surge overnight toward 113 yen, into an area where many dealers had been short options for months.

"A few month ago, you would have had to be very bullish to expect these levels, but now you're within reach of 115," said a U.S. bank dealer in New York. He expected more short-covering to emerge as the dollar rumbled higher.

Dealers said the perceived trend change started at the back end last week, when the London arm of a large U.S. investment bank continuously bid for six-month yen puts with strike prices of about 120 yen.
Traders were puzzled about the investment bank's intentions but the large amount of buying caught many off guard and stirred interest in covering short positions.

"People are buying lottery tickets with those low-delta options," said a trader at a European bank in Chicago. He said the back end had been oversold in recent months and that there should have been some natural bid.
Okada at DKB said he suspected the purchases were not just simple currency trading.
"If you want to make a directional bet, the 115-yen strike seems like a more realistic target," he said.

A six-month 120-yen yen put would have a delta value of around five to seven which means potential increases in the delta -- and therefore premium -- would be very slow even if the spot market moved in their favor.
Traders said the Japanese general elections at the weekend had little impact on the market but that the outcome probably favored the status quo and the dollar's bullishness.

Risk reversals, which compare pricing for puts and calls, narrowed as demand for yen puts increased. One-month 25-delta dollar/yen, which had been sharply skewed toward yen calls for most of the year, stood at around par.
Dollar/mark volatilities were higher across the board but were little changed from Thursday's levels prior to Friday's pre-weekend decay.
"Spot's not moving enough in dollar/mark to warrant volatilities being higher," the European bank trader said.
One-month dollar/mark implied volatility regained a few tenths of a point from late Friday levels to 6.8/6.9 percent.
-- Shin Kishima/Chicago Derivatives Desk (312) 408-8750
